name: Carnivore-ish / animal-based diet

lead: The animal-based diet centres on ruminant meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and often raw dairy, with limited fruit and honey for carbohydrate, and no vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts or seeds. People follow it for clearer skin, better sleep and energy, and a leaner physique.

The chain is nutrient-dense animal foods, with fruit and honey adding energy, so eating stays simple while nutrient needs are covered. Psychiatrist Paul Saladino popularised it in the early 2020s as a looser form of strict carnivore, after reporting low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone on strict carnivore. Short-term feeding research shows an all-animal diet changes gut bacteria within days, and no trial has tested the full pattern. Looksmax.org users post both enthusiastic essays and reports of poor sleep, fatigue and acne after a year.

paras: Plates are built around beef, organ meats, eggs and fish, with fruit and honey for carbohydrate and sometimes raw dairy. Many people treat it as an easier version of carnivore, and report changes in digestion and energy over weeks to months.
Concerns raised include missing fibre and plant nutrients, high saturated fat, and the food-safety risk of raw dairy. Mainstream nutrition experts call the diet restrictive.

chain: Clearer skin, leaner, more energy claimed
angle.text: Followers eat meat, organs, fruit and honey for clearer skin, better sleep, energy and a leaner physique, on the idea that nutrient-dense animal foods cover their needs. Evidence is mostly testimonials, and no trial has tested the whole pattern.

lead: The animal-based diet emphasises nutrient-dense animal products such as meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and raw dairy, with limited low-toxicity fruits and honey, while excluding vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds.[1] Wikipedia describes it as a looser variant of the carnivore diet, adding fruit, honey and raw dairy, and credits Paul Saladino with popularising it.[2] People in appearance communities adopt it for the body and skin they hope it produces: a leaner, more muscular physique from high protein intake and organ-meat nutrients, clearer skin and better energy and sleep, and higher testosterone, which proponents link with a more masculine look.[1][3]

Saladino, a psychiatrist, wrote The Carnivore Code in 2020, founded the organ-supplement company Heart & Soil that year, and later shifted from strict carnivore to an approach including fruit and honey, saying strict carnivore had left him with low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone.[1][4] Proponents claim improved digestion, mental clarity and chronic disease management, whereas mainstream nutrition experts regard the diet as restrictive with potential long-term risks.[1][2]

The research record is limited to related studies: a 2021 survey of 2,029 self-selected carnivore dieters, short-term microbiome feeding trials, nutrient-adequacy modelling, and reviews of carnivore eating in sport; no trial has tested the animal-based pattern as a whole.[5][6][6][7] On looksmax.org the diet is discussed both as an optimal human diet in long essays and as a disappointment by users reporting poor sleep, fatigue and acne after about a year.[3][8]

paras: Ruminant meats such as beef and lamb form the base, with organ meats (liver, heart) as staples, fish and seafood, eggs and dairy that advocates prefer raw or minimally processed, and limited fruit such as berries and avocado plus honey.[1] Strict versions keep fruit and honey minimal; inclusive versions add more of these carbohydrate sources, and people with dairy intolerance may use A2 milk.[1]

Vegetables are omitted because of oxalates and lectins, and grains, legumes, nuts and seeds because of phytates and fibre, according to proponents.[1] Grokipedia reports that proponents argue organ meats supply enough vitamin C to prevent scurvy, that heme iron and zinc from red meat are well absorbed, and that preformed vitamin A from liver avoids the conversion step needed for plant beta-carotene.[1] It also gives illustrative daily macronutrient ranges used by advocates and describes the pattern as used by athletes for weight gain with a calorie surplus.[1]

Wikipedia places the animal-based diet in a family that includes the strict carnivore diet, the beef-only lion diet and carnivore traditionalism, which favours regeneratively raised livestock and eggs under the motto that it is not the cow but the how.[2]

Wikipedia traces exclusively animal-based eating through 19th-century figures: Bernard Moncriff, who published The Philosophy of the Stomach in 1856 and lived a year on beef and milk; the Italian physician Arnaldo Cantani, who prescribed an animal-based diet for diabetic patients in the 1870s; and James H. Salisbury, whose meat-and-hot-water regimen was popular in the 1880s.[2] Grokipedia also cites the Inuit and Maasai and Vilhjalmur Stefansson's supervised meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital in 1928.[1]

The carnivore diet gained renewed attention around 2018 when former orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker promoted it on social media and wrote The Carnivore Diet, and when Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila reported a beef-only version that later went viral on TikTok.[2] The animal-based variant emerged after 2020 as a version adding low-toxin plant foods, spread through podcasts, books, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and Discord communities.[1][2]

Saladino hosts the Fundamental Health podcast, formerly the Paul Saladino MD podcast.[1] Wikipedia's biography of Saladino reports that he was born in 1977, earned his MD at the University of Arizona in 2015, completed a psychiatry residency at the University of Washington in 2019, and was vegan before becoming a leading advocate of strict carnivore eating.[4] His 2020 book The Carnivore Code was described by The New Yorker as the closest thing the Paleo movement has to a manifesto, and he said that the diet cured his anxiety and eczema.[4] While on the diet he reported sleep disturbances, palpitations, cramps and lower testosterone, and by 2020 had added fruit and honey, calling the resulting pattern animal-based.[4] His appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience in 2020 greatly expanded his audience.[4]

In 2022 Saladino and fellow carnivore advocate Anthony Gustin visited the Hadza in Tanzania, presenting them as a dietary model, and in 2023 he collaborated with the Los Angeles grocer Erewhon on a raw animal-based smoothie.[4] Wikipedia notes that traditionalist carnivore advocates focus on regeneratively raised livestock and that the meat-influencer movement has been described as fringe.[2]

Heart & Soil is an Austin, Texas supplement company selling encapsulated organ-meat products, co-owned by Saladino and the fitness influencer Brian Johnson, known as the Liver King.[4][9] Johnson promotes an ancestral lifestyle built around raw meat and organs; in late 2022 leaked emails led him to acknowledge steroid use after he had denied it, an episode that critics cited when discussing claims that such physiques come from diet alone.[9]

Grokipedia also names Shawn Baker and the family physician Ken Berry as promoters of related meat-centric or low-carbohydrate approaches, and notes that its own source base is weighted toward proponents and affiliated companies.[1] A 2026 content analysis of 1,169 Instagram posts by 19 carnivore content creators found that they portrayed the diet positively, emphasised red meat and frequently made health and disease claims alongside political and anti-institutional themes.[6]

No clinical trial has tested the animal-based diet as a whole. Related research includes a 2014 Nature study in which short-term consumption of diets made entirely of animal or plant products altered the gut microbial community and gene expression within days, with the animal-based diet increasing bile-tolerant bacteria.[5]

Two crossover or parallel studies tested supplements alongside animal-based feeding: cranberry powder over five days in 11 healthy adults attenuated diet-induced microbiota changes,[10] and a probiotic yoghurt study examined changes in gut microbiota during an animal-based diet.[11]

Observational research on the opposite pattern found that, in the Rotterdam Study, greater adherence to a plant-based diet was associated with lower insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.[12] Such findings concern diet patterns in general populations and do not test carnivore-style eating directly.

Wikipedia reports that nutrition scientists, dietitians and physicians regard carnivore diets as extreme fads, citing lack of fibre, micronutrient shortfalls, raised LDL cholesterol and links between high red-meat intake and colon cancer and gout, and that the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet.[2] Neurologist Steven Novella described it in 2023 as the latest fad diet.[2]
No studies found of the animal-based diet as a complete pattern. The nearest research concerns the stricter carnivore diet and short-term feeding in healthy volunteers.[5][10][11]

A 2021 descriptive survey in Current Developments in Nutrition, recruited through social media between March and June 2020, included 2,029 adults who said they had eaten a carnivore diet for at least six months (median age 44, 67 percent male). Participants reported high satisfaction, with 95 percent reporting overall health improvement, a fall in median BMI from 27.2 to 24.3, and low rates of adverse effects, including dermatologic symptoms in 0.1 to 1.9 percent. In a subset with lab results, LDL cholesterol was markedly elevated at a mean of 172 mg/dL. The authors noted that self-selected, self-reported data cannot establish causation or long-term safety.[6]

A 2025 exploratory German study of 24 people on a self-designed carnivore diet reported subjective improvements and significant rises in total and LDL cholesterol, with LDL from 157 to 256 mg/dL on average, while some participants with high triglycerides or pre-diabetic HbA1c saw those values fall.[6]

A 2026 scoping review of nine human studies of the carnivore diet reported short-term weight loss, satiety and some changes in inflammatory or metabolic markers, along with risks of deficiencies in vitamins C and D, calcium, magnesium, iodine and fibre and raised LDL and total cholesterol; the authors called the evidence quality very limited.[6] A 2024 nutrient analysis of four hypothetical carnivore meal plans found they met reference values for B12, zinc and vitamin A but fell short for thiamin, magnesium, calcium, vitamin C and fibre.[7]

A 2026 narrative review of carnivore and animal-based diets in sport concluded that carbohydrate restriction may raise fat oxidation without reliably improving performance in high-intensity training, and raised concerns about micronutrient adequacy, gut microbiota and lipid profiles.[13][6] Published case reports include a man who developed acute pancreatitis from severe hypertriglyceridemia while on a carnivore diet and, separately, a patient who reported diabetes remission; single cases cannot establish cause.[6]

Raw dairy is a distinctive element of Saladino's version. Wikipedia's raw milk article reports that raw milk can carry pathogens such as Campylobacter, Listeria, Salmonella and E. coli, that children under five, adults over 65, pregnant women and immunocompromised people are at particular risk, and that the CDC and FDA strongly recommend against consuming raw milk or raw milk products; proponents cite taste, nutrition and immune benefits, which the article says have not been clearly demonstrated.[14]

Saladino has drawn criticism for promoting raw milk. Wikipedia reports that in May 2024 he posted a video promoting raw dairy for infants that drew strong backlash and was removed the next day, and that in May 2025 he appeared in a video with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. drinking raw milk with honey; the raw milk supplier for the 2023 Erewhon smoothie later switched to pasteurisation after H5N1 testing.[4]

Raw milk sale rules vary: about 43 US states allow some form of sale, the FDA bans interstate sale for human consumption, and in the UK retail sale has been banned since 1985 while registered farms may sell it directly.[14]

A looksmax.org thread presents a long, AI-assisted essay arguing that evolutionary, isotopic and clinical evidence supports an animal-based whole-food diet and that mainstream dietary advice rests on low-quality evidence.[3] A separate thread titled as a failure report describes about a year of eating a pound of meat, organs and fruit under 100 grams of carbohydrate, with worse sleep, low energy, ongoing cystic acne and bloating; replies include an unrelated claim that meat acidifies the body.[8]
A T Nation member announced plans to follow an animal-based diet closely for a month alongside a swing challenge, an example of its spread in physique-training circles.[15]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org post both advocacy and failure reports about the animal-based diet.[3][8]

claims.claim: An animal-based diet is the optimal human diet.
It clears acne and fixes sleep and energy.
The diet failed for some users.
Eating only meat acidifies the body, while vegetables alkalise.
Plants contain toxins such as lectins and oxalates that are best avoided.
Raw dairy is healthier than pasteurised dairy.
Meat and organs build muscle and testosterone for a better physique.

timeline.event: Bernard Moncriff publishes The Philosophy of the Stomach and spends a year on beef and milk.[2]
Arnaldo Cantani prescribes an animal-based diet to diabetic patients.[2]
James H. Salisbury promotes a meat-and-hot-water regimen.[2]
Vilhjalmur Stefansson completes a supervised meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital.[1]
A Nature study reports that animal-based diets alter gut microbiota within days.[5]
Shawn Baker publishes The Carnivore Diet and the diet gains online attention; Jordan Peterson and his daughter adopt a beef-only version.[1][2]
Paul Saladino publishes The Carnivore Code, founds Heart & Soil, appears on Joe Rogan's podcast and adds fruit and honey to his diet.[1][4]
A survey of 2,029 carnivore dieters is published in Current Developments in Nutrition.[6]
Saladino visits the Hadza in Tanzania; Liver King acknowledges steroid use after leaked emails.[4][9]
Saladino collaborates with Erewhon on a raw animal-based smoothie.[4]
Saladino posts, then removes, a video promoting raw dairy for infants.[4]
Saladino appears in a raw milk video with Robert F. Kennedy Jr.[4]
A scoping review of nine carnivore diet studies and a review of carnivore diets in sport are published.[6][13]
